summary: PACE measures the token cost of compiling repeated GUI (computer-use) procedures into parameterized programs, including failed compilation attempts, and proposes an online rent-or-buy style algorithm that decides when to compile under a cumulative (1+epsilon) cost budget relative to always running the agent. Savings are shown mainly in simulations that map measured cost profiles onto synthetic grids and recorded public event-log arrival orders.

claims.claim: Payback counts for successful compilations are 2-16 uses (excluding source agent runs).
claims.evidence: Table 1 compilation-only payback ranges 1.39 to 15.5 uses (text: 1.389 to 15.488); abstract rounds up. Only 11 of 20 compilation cells pass verification; seven task families, three models, k=3 source traces.

claims.claim: PACE reduces token cost by 17.3% vs ReAct, 24.9% vs AutoRPA adaptation, 17.3% vs ToolPro adaptation on recorded arrivals (eps=0.25).
claims.evidence: §5.1: 17.34% vs ReAct, CI [14.96,19.61]%; Table 3 ratios. These are simulations: logs (Sepsis, BPI 2019, two Wikipedia streams) supply arrival order only; measured cost profiles are shuffled onto families. PACE is costlier than ReAct in 3 of 12 conditions (Sepsis ratios 0.971-0.998). ToolPro equals ReAct by construction in grids. Authors state the grids were used while developing PACE.

claims.claim: Cumulative cost never exceeds (1+eps) times agent-only cost.
claims.evidence: Theorem 4.1 with proof under stated action-cost bounds; empirically all 4800 grid runs and 120 log runs stay within 1.25. Limitations note historical mean costs do not provide the required bounds.

claims.claim: The savings test and failed-attempt cost accounting matter; the budget mainly protects worst case.
claims.evidence: Table 4: removing savings test raises log mean cost 52.68%; equal attempt costs +23.34%; removing budget changes log mean by 0.0013% but raises worst grid ratio from 1.2468 to 1.7563.

patterns.note: Explicit cumulative token budget with provable bound; ablation shows it caps worst-case overspend.
Compiling agent traces into executable programs cuts per-use cost (saving shares 0.936-0.999), with agent fallback.
Trace-to-deterministic-program is analogous to recipe codification; compilation fails in 9/20 cells and failed attempts cost ~6.6x successful ones (DeepSeek median).
Measurement protocol records successful and failed compilation charges; useful cost-accounting template.

methodology.sample: 7 task families (4 AndroidWorld, 2 custom LibreOffice in OSWorld container, 1 WebArena Reddit); 30 fresh deployment tasks per program; 180 matched agent replays; simulations over 2x300 conditions x 8 runs and 12 log conditions x 10 runs.
methodology.baselines: ReAct (always agent), decision-rule adaptations of AutoRPA and ToolPro using the same compiler; not original systems end to end. ToolPro degenerates to ReAct in grids.
methodology.models: GLM 5.3 Flash, DeepSeek Flash, Qwen 3.8 Flash (cheap tier only).
methodology.variance: Paired bootstrap (2000 resamples) conditional CIs in App. C.7/C.8; compilation itself mostly single attempt with a repeated-compilation appendix.
methodology.ablations: No savings test, no budget, equal attempt costs, eager retry; cost-ratio sensitivity over 72 conditions.
methodology.contamination_controls: n/a (cost measurement); authors flag that simulation grids were used during development so not independent confirmation.
methodology.languages: Generated programs for GUI automation; no software-engineering code tasks.

standards.peer_review: arXiv preprint, no venue listed (comment: 27 pages, 3 figures).
standards.artifacts: Code, saved records, and scripts claimed at github.com/myl7/computer-use.

biases.detail: Headline savings come from simulations mapping measured cost profiles onto arrival logs from non-GUI process logs; live study (App. D) tests only fallback for a fixed program, not the online algorithm (§7).
Seven task families, 11 verified programs; payback range rests on a handful of cells in Table 1.
Baselines are decision-rule adaptations; ToolPro adaptation is identical to ReAct in grids, making the '17.3% vs ToolPro' headline a repeat of the ReAct number.
Authors state the grids were used while developing PACE (§5).
Latency, device use, and program-maintenance effort excluded (§7).

coi.affiliations: City University of Hong Kong (all four authors per authors block).
coi.vendor_products_evaluated: None owned by authors; uses third-party GLM/DeepSeek/Qwen models.
coi.detail: Academic authors evaluating their own algorithm (usual self-evaluation), no vendor interest.

verdict_reason: Careful cost accounting with a proved budget bound and candid limitations, but savings are simulated, tested on cheap models and GUI tasks only, and baselines are weak adaptations; relevance to a code harness is indirect.
applicability: Indirect for a Java backend team. The transferable idea is the accounting rule: before codifying a repeated agent procedure (e.g., a recurring content-ingestion transformation across the several repositories) into a deterministic script or recipe, count failed codification attempts and expected reuse, and cap cumulative spend relative to just letting the agent do it. That suggests a harness-level token budget per task family and a 'promote to script after N successful repeats' rule that works regardless of which agent host is used. GUI-specific results (screenshots, AndroidWorld) do not transfer, and nothing here addresses Java, multi-repo contracts, or spec-driven development.
